source: Wikipedia: Monte Carlo tree search (disadvantages section)
finding: Lists MCTS limits: the basic form converges only in 'Monte Carlo perfect' games, trap states are missed because of selective expansion, and heuristics need many parameters.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Ramanujan, Sabharwal and Selman 2010 and Ramanujan and Selman 2011 for traps. Says the AlphaGo loss in game 4 against Lee Sedol may be partly due to this.
quote: MCTS may not 'see' such lines due to its policy of selective node expansion
limits: Encyclopedia summary; the AlphaGo link is described as belief, not proven.
agent_relevance: Our focus row 'can miss trap states; many parameters' comes from here. Treat a search that samples few lines as blind to narrow refutations.

source: Ramanujan, Sabharwal, Selman (2010) On Adversarial Search Spaces and Sampling-Based Planning (ICAPS)
finding: Defines a level-k search trap: a move after which the opponent has a k-move forced win. Shallow traps (levels 3-7) are common in Chess, even in grandmaster games, but rare in Go. This explains why UCT wins in Go and loses to minimax in Chess.
numbers: Semi-random games: about 7-10% of 31-ply boards and up to 15% of 47-ply boards have a trap at levels 1-7. 200 grandmaster games: about 12% at 47 ply. 200 games per condition.
quote: UCT has a good chance of missing even very shallow traps and thus losing the game
limits: Chess evaluation only; trap frequency was measured, not tied to full-game win rates. 4-page short paper.
agent_relevance: Our agent's search over reasoning steps is safe only if the domain has few shallow traps. Where a single wrong step is fatal, add exhaustive checks.

source: Ramanujan et al. (2010) UCT utility of trap moves (Table 1, Fig 3)
finding: UCT gives a trap move almost the same value as the best move at trap levels 5 and 7, so it cannot tell a forced loss from a good move. Level 3 is detected.
numbers: Utility in [-1,1], ideal trap value -1. Level-3 trap: UCT-best -0.083, minimax-depth-7 best -0.092, trap move -0.250. Level-5: +0.020, +0.013, -0.012. Level-7: -0.056, -0.063, -0.066 (as extracted; a further row +0.011, +0.009, +0.004 also appears). UCT exploration constant 0.4. Four boards only.
limits: Only four example boards in the table. Row labels are ambiguous in the text extraction.
agent_relevance: A mean-value estimate hides rare fatal branches. Do not trust averaged scores of sampled continuations as proof that a step is safe (supports G3, G4).

source: Ramanujan et al. (2010) More samples do not fix it (Fig 5, Fig 4)
finding: Even with 10x the nodes minimax needs, UCT's value for a level-5 or level-7 trap stays high (above -0.15). UCT spends about 70% of its time deeper than level 5 when a level-5 trap exists. Wasted depth grows exponentially with trap depth.
numbers: Value stays above -0.15 at 10x minimax nodes (sometimes 50x, data not shown). About 70% of iterations explore deeper than needed.
limits: Chess boards, one UCT setting.
agent_relevance: More sampling budget is not a cure for missing a narrow refutation. Use a different kind of check (exhaustive or verified) instead of more rollouts.

source: Coquelin, Munos (2007) Bandit Algorithms for Tree Search
finding: UCT is O(log n) regret in the limit but its early phase can be extremely bad. On a hard tree of depth D the number of plays before it finds the good branch is doubly exponential in D. It is too optimistic and may take a very long time to find good branches that looked bad at first.
numbers: With the square-root confidence term, regret lower bound is Omega(exp(exp(D))); with the usual log term it is a composition of D-1 exponentials. Their fix gives worst-case regret of order 2^D / sqrt(n)-type scaling with smoothness. Example D=20 gives an astronomically large number.
limits: Worst-case construction, not a typical tree. Analysis is for bandit trees with a stationary-leaf setup.
agent_relevance: Formal reason MCTS fails in deep, deceptive trees: early bad-looking branches get starved. Keep depth shallow and use a shallow exhaustive pass for branches that look bad.

source: Coquelin, Munos (2007) Modified UCT and exploration schedule
finding: Fix: widen the confidence interval for nodes near the root, so exploration is higher where the bias of the estimates decays slowly. Flat UCB on the leaves still costs exponential in depth.
numbers: Flat UCB over 2^D leaves has regret that depends exponentially on D. Under a smoothness assumption the modified tree bound is better, as stated in the paper intro.
limits: Needs knowledge of smoothness constants, which are unknown in language search.
agent_relevance: Shows the exploration parameters matter a lot, which is the 'many parameters' risk. No safe default exists across trees.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play (AlphaZero)
finding: With a learned policy and value network, MCTS beat Stockfish and Elmo, so the earlier chess weakness of plain UCT went away once the network guided the search. AlphaZero's MCTS scaled better with thinking time than alpha-beta.
numbers: AlphaZero searches 80 thousand positions per second in chess and 40 thousand in shogi, versus 70 million for Stockfish and 35 million for Elmo. Lost zero games to Stockfish in the main match and eight to Elmo.
quote: calling into question the widely held belief that alpha-beta search is inherently superior in these domains
limits: Needed a huge training run (self-play, TPUs). Does not remove traps in principle; the network supplies the missing prior. Draws compress the Elo scale in chess.
agent_relevance: MCTS works when a strong learned value exists. A prompted LLM judge is not that. The limit is value quality, not the search loop.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs (ICML)
finding: A trained adversary beats KataGo, a superhuman MCTS agent, by exploiting a blind spot (cyclic groups), not by playing Go well. The attack works at superhuman search settings and transfers zero-shot to other Go AIs.
numbers: Pass-adversary: 99.9% vs no-search KataGo. Cyclic-adversary: 100% (1048/1048) vs defended Latest with no search, 95.7% (1007/1052) with 4096 visits, 72% with 10^7 visits. Under 14% of KataGo training compute. The adversary loses to amateur humans.
quote: our adversaries do not win by playing Go well
limits: Gray-box access to the victim network. Go only. Human experts could copy the strategy.
agent_relevance: Even huge search does not remove systematic value-model blind spots. Search amplifies a model, it does not fix its blind spots (supports G4, G3).

source: Tseng et al. (2025) Can Go AIs Be Adversarially Robust?
finding: Three defenses (adversarial training on hand-made positions, iterated adversarial training, a ViT architecture) did not hold against fresh adversaries. Most working attacks were variants of the cyclic attack.
numbers: Text reports adversary win rates such as 81% using 5% of the victim's compute, 90% using 26% of defense compute, 42% against the iterated-defense victim v9, but only 4% at 4096 visits. Exact setting per number not fully mapped.
limits: Several figures are read from the intro text; high victim visits lowers adversary win rate but does not remove it.
agent_relevance: Patching one failure leaves the class. A scaffold should not assume a patched case closes the class (supports G3 held-out checks).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Adversarial policies: finding on search budget
finding: More victim search lowers but does not kill the exploit: the win rate falls from 95.7% (4096 visits) to 72% (10 million visits). Search gives diminishing but not zero protection.
numbers: 95.7% at 4096 visits versus 72% at 10^7 visits for the cyclic adversary against Latest-def.
limits: Single attack family, one victim network lineage.
agent_relevance: Test-time compute has a ceiling set by the quality of the evaluator.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1, Appendix: unsuccessful attempts (MCTS)
finding: The team tried MCTS with a pre-trained value model for reasoning and gave up as a training method. The token space is exponentially larger than chess. A per-node extension cap leads to local optima. A fine-grained value model is hard to train. MCTS helps at inference only when paired with a pre-trained value model.
numbers: No benchmark numbers given for the failed attempt. Process reward models had three limits: step definition, step correctness, reward hacking.
quote: unlike chess, where the search space is relatively well-defined, token generation presents an exponentially larger search space
limits: They state this does not mean the approaches cannot work. Qualitative report, no ablation table.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence from a frontier lab that tree search over free-form reasoning is hard to make pay. Prefer a few sampled attempts plus code-checked selection.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally
finding: Against a process reward model on MATH, beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets but the gain shrinks and often reverses at large budgets. Lookahead search (a special case of MCTS-style rollouts) generally underperforms at the same generation budget.
numbers: Lookahead cost counted as N x (k+1) samples. Budgets from 4 to 256 generations. Beam search over-optimizes on easy questions (levels 1-2) and helps on medium ones (levels 3-4).
quote: search causes the model to generate low-information repetitive steps at the end of a solution
limits: PRM-guided, MATH only; exploitation of PRM errors is the stated reason. Not an exact MCTS run.
agent_relevance: Search helps only on medium-hard items and hurts when the verifier is imperfect. Use a difficulty gate; keep to plain sampling on easy items.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Inference Scaling Laws (ICLR) REBASE vs MCTS
finding: Standard MCTS did not do well with weighted voting under equal compute; MCTS uses dozens of times more tokens because many rollout paths never reach the final answer set. Their cheaper tree search REBASE beat both sampling and MCTS.
numbers: Table 1 (MATH500, weighted voting): Mistral-7B sampling 256 samples 42.8% at 8.70e14 FLOPs vs REBASE 32 samples 45.0% at 1.36e14; Llemma-7B 45.5% vs 46.8%; Llemma-34B 46.7% vs 49.2% (12.1e14 vs 7.08e14, as extracted).
quote: MCTS consumes substantially more resources, often requiring dozens of times more generated tokens
limits: Cost counted in FLOPs on MATH500/GSM8K with Llemma and Mistral; MCTS baseline details are in later sections.
agent_relevance: Rollout-based value estimates waste budget. A reward-balanced tree with no rollouts can be cheaper. Keep search cost in the budget.

source: Wu et al. (2025) Saturation of sampling
finding: Accuracy from sampling saturates for a fixed model; the saturation limit is set by the model's own probability of correct answers. A smaller model with better search can match a larger one at lower compute.
numbers: Theory in Appendix A: saturation at high sampling budgets. The 7B model beats the 34B model until 128 Llemma-7B solutions are sampled.
limits: Math reasoning only.
agent_relevance: More search cannot exceed what the base model puts probability on; hard items need a different move (reframe, tool), not more depth.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: MCTS with the LLM as world model and reward lifts planning in Blocksworld, with the largest gain on short plans and a steep fall at 6 steps.
numbers: LLaMA-33B Blocksworld success: CoT 0.17/0.02/0.00 (2/4/6 steps); RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42; GPT-4 CoT 0.50/0.63/0.40. Average 64%. GSM8K: CoT 29.4, RAP(1) 48.6, RAP(10) 51.6 (table columns partly garbled in extraction). PrOntoQA proof accuracy 78.8 vs 64.8 for CoT.
limits: LLM self-reward is noisy; 20 iterations; trimmed history for reward makes the last steps easier (paper notes this).
agent_relevance: MCTS over LLM states helps on small search spaces; the 6-step result shows the limit as the space grows.

source: Hao et al. (2023) RAP search space note
finding: The 6-step Blocksworld search space can be as large as 5^6 (text extraction shows '56'), and RAP with 20 iterations finds a plan 42% of the time. Doubling iterations from 10 to 20 lifted 6-step success from 0.26 to 0.42, so success depends on budget.
numbers: 0.26 at 10 iterations, 0.42 at 20 iterations for 6-step problems.
limits: Budget-hungry; no trap analysis.
agent_relevance: Budget-vs-depth tradeoff: success at depth needs many iterations.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: MCTS with LM value, self-reflection and environment feedback. State-of-the-art on HumanEval with GPT-4, better than ToT and RAP on HotPotQA at equal node budget. The authors list higher compute cost and the need to revert states as limits.
numbers: 92.7 Pass@1 on HumanEval (GPT-4). HotPotQA: ReAct best k=250 0.42; CoT-SC 0.40; LATS (n=1,k=50) 0.48; ToT 0.49; RAP 0.54; LATS (n=5,k=50) 0.63. Token use on success: RAP 210,215 vs LATS 176,500 (as extracted).
limits: Uses ground-truth test or environment feedback; the gain depends on it. Reversible states assumed.
agent_relevance: Search pays off when real feedback (tests) exists. This fits our code-checked guardrails G2 and G3.

source: Feng et al. (2023) AlphaZero-like Tree-Search can Guide LLM Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: A learned value function guides tree search; prior LLM work (ToT, RAP) used prompt-based values that are unreliable. Learned-value MCTS variants reach good accuracy per compute among search types tested.
numbers: Reports Path@1 and multi-path results on GSM8K, Game24, PrOntoQA, RLHF alignment; Game24 ToT with GPT-3.5 gets 15.5 vs 19.1 with the learned LLaMA value (as extracted from Table 2). MCTS is almost the best for performance and cost when searching several paths.
limits: Requires training a value network per task; in Path@1, search degenerates to greedy value search.
agent_relevance: Value quality is the key lever. Without a trained value, tree search buys little.

source: Qi et al. (2024) rStar: mutual reasoning makes smaller LLMs stronger
finding: Plain MCTS with a small model's own self-evaluation gives minimal gains. Adding human-like action types and a second model that verifies trajectories fixes much of this.
numbers: GSM8K LLaMA2-7B 12.51% to 63.91% with rStar (32 MCTS rollouts); another model 36.46% to 81.88%. Text says traditional MCTS yields minimal improvement with small models.
limits: Needs a second discriminator model; gains are measured against few-shot CoT baselines.
agent_relevance: Self-evaluation inside the search is weak. Use an independent check, not the same model grading itself.

source: Koh et al. (2024) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Best-first tree search with an LM value function lifts web-agent success. Gains grow with search budget, and both depth and breadth must grow together.
numbers: VisualWebArena: GPT-4o + SoM 18.9% to 26.4% (+39.7% relative). WebArena: +28.0% relative to 19.2%. Llama-3-70B + captions 7.6% to 16.7% (+119.7%). Search capped at 5 actions beat the no-search baseline with 30 actions. 910 VWA and 812 WA tasks.
limits: Search limited to depth 5 by compute; reversible environment assumed; low absolute success rates.
agent_relevance: Search over actions with an outside success signal works. Depth and breadth must scale together.

source: Kocsis, Szepesvari (2006) Bandit based Monte-Carlo planning (UCT)
finding: Introduced UCT: apply UCB1 at each tree node, prove convergence to the minimax value in the limit. Not opened this session; cited second-hand via Ramanujan 2010 and Coquelin 2007.
numbers: No numbers recorded from this source.
limits: The finite-time behavior is not covered by the convergence proof (see Coquelin and Munos 2007).
agent_relevance: Origin of the exploration parameter C that has to be tuned per domain.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: UCB1 gives logarithmic regret for stationary bandits. UCT reuses it at inner nodes where reward distributions drift. Not opened; cited in Ramanujan 2010 and Coquelin 2007.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Stationary rewards assumed.
agent_relevance: Coquelin and Munos say the UCT bounds are not true upper bounds in trees.

source: Browne et al. (2012) A Survey of Monte Carlo Tree Search Methods
finding: Standard survey, cited by Wikipedia for UCT convergence to minimax and for the trap-state weakness. Not opened this session.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Reference list of MCTS enhancements, many of which add parameters.

source: Silver et al. (2016) Mastering the game of Go (AlphaGo) and Lee Sedol game 4
finding: Wikipedia's MCTS page says the game 4 loss to Lee Sedol may be partly due to a missed narrow line. Not opened; claim is second-hand and unproven.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Cause of the game 4 loss is a belief, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: Even a strong MCTS agent had a visible miss on a narrow refutation.

source: Wikipedia MCTS page: convergence note (Althofer 2012, Monte Carlo perfect games)
finding: The basic algorithm converges only in 'Monte Carlo perfect' games per Althofer (2012); UCT converges to minimax per Kocsis and Szepesvari. The guarantee depends on the variant, and is asymptotic.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Page summary only; Althofer paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not quote asymptotic guarantees as if they cover our small budgets.

source: Wu et al. (2025) MCTS vs best-of-n cost framing
finding: Generic comparisons of MCTS with best-of-n and majority voting in generated tokens or time are scarce, and those that exist point to an unfavorable cost-performance trade-off.
numbers: No single figure; claim is about tokens being 'dozens of times' higher.
limits: Authors' background claim in section 3.1.1.
agent_relevance: Count total tokens including rollouts before choosing tree search over plain sampling.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Difficulty-bin analysis of search
finding: Beam search over-optimizes the PRM on easy questions (levels 1-2) at higher budgets while it helps on medium problems (levels 3-4). Search helps most where the base model sometimes, not never, succeeds.
numbers: Bars at 4, 16, 64, 256 generations per difficulty bin on MATH.
limits: Single PRM; the hardest bin is mostly unsolved by any method.
agent_relevance: Gate search on estimated difficulty; skip on easy and on hopeless items.
